profile.subject: Ludwig van Beethoven
profile.overview: Ludwig van Beethoven was a composer and pianist from Bonn who made his career in Vienna, where he first drew attention by improvising at the keyboard. As his hearing deteriorated, he kept composing, writing piano sonatas, string quartets and symphonies that stretched the musical forms he had inherited.

key_moments.title: From Bonn to Vienna
key_moments.text: Beethoven left Bonn to study with **Joseph Haydn** in Vienna. He had gone there to learn composition, but the skill that first caught Viennese audiences' attention was making music up at the piano.
claims: Ludwig van Beethoven moved from Bonn to Vienna in 1792.
Ludwig van Beethoven studied composition with Joseph Haydn in Vienna.
Ludwig van Beethoven gained an early reputation in Vienna for improvising at the piano.

key_moments.title: A letter kept private
key_moments.text: At **Heiligenstadt** outside Vienna, Beethoven wrote to his brothers about the isolation his worsening hearing had brought. He said that thoughts of the music he still wanted to write had kept him from taking his own life. The letter stayed among his papers and was discovered after his death.
claims: Ludwig van Beethoven wrote the Heiligenstadt Testament to his brothers in 1802 while staying in Heiligenstadt outside Vienna.
Ludwig van Beethoven described his isolation over his hearing loss in the Heiligenstadt Testament.
Ludwig van Beethoven said in the Heiligenstadt Testament that his art had kept him from taking his own life.
The Heiligenstadt Testament was found among Ludwig van Beethoven's papers after his death.

key_moments.title: The Eroica reaches the public
key_moments.text: Vienna's **Theater an der Wien** hosted the first public performance of Beethoven's **Third Symphony**. Its length alone pushed beyond what listeners expected of a symphony at the time. In the middle of a work now known as the *Eroica*, or heroic symphony, Beethoven placed a funeral march.
claims: Ludwig van Beethoven's Third Symphony received its first public performance at the Theater an der Wien in 1805.
Ludwig van Beethoven's Third Symphony was unusually long for a symphony of its time.
Ludwig van Beethoven's Third Symphony is known as the Eroica, meaning heroic.
The second movement of Ludwig van Beethoven's Third Symphony is a funeral march.

key_moments.title: Voices enter the Ninth
key_moments.text: An orchestra premiered Beethoven's **Ninth Symphony** in Vienna. The first three movements were entirely instrumental. Then solo singers and a choir joined the orchestra for the finale, singing words from **Friedrich Schiller's** poem *Ode to Joy*.
claims: Ludwig van Beethoven's Ninth Symphony premiered in Vienna in 1824.
The first three movements of Ludwig van Beethoven's Ninth Symphony are instrumental.
The finale of Ludwig van Beethoven's Ninth Symphony features vocal soloists and a choir singing words from Friedrich Schiller's Ode to Joy.

deep_facts.text: Visitors could talk to Beethoven by writing in a notebook. He often answered aloud, so the surviving conversation books can preserve a friend's words while leaving Beethoven's side of the exchange to the imagination.
claims: Ludwig van Beethoven's visitors wrote their remarks in conversation books because of Ludwig van Beethoven's hearing loss.
Ludwig van Beethoven often answered visitors aloud, leaving only the visitors' side in many surviving conversation book exchanges.

deep_facts.text: The publisher Anton Diabelli invited composers to write a variation on a waltz he had supplied. Beethoven produced 33. That single waltz became the material for a whole piano work, the *Diabelli Variations*.
claims: Music publisher Anton Diabelli invited composers to write a variation on a waltz composed by Anton Diabelli.
Ludwig van Beethoven's Diabelli Variations consist of 33 piano variations on Anton Diabelli's waltz.

deep_facts.text: The opening movement of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony traveled into space on the Voyager Golden Record. The music chosen for the spacecraft also included a quieter piece by Beethoven, the Cavatina from his String Quartet No. 13.
claims: The Voyager Golden Record carried aboard the Voyager spacecraft includes the opening movement of Ludwig van Beethoven's Fifth Symphony.
The Voyager Golden Record includes the Cavatina from Ludwig van Beethoven's String Quartet No. 13.

key_moments.0.text: The evidence establishes an early reputation as a performer and improviser in Viennese salons, but does not identify improvisation alone as the first skill to attract audiences. Use the documented early reputation.

key_moments.1.text: The cited passages document his seclusion and the letter’s despair, but do not show him describing social isolation in the letter itself. Use the Testament text or say he wrote about his worsening hearing and despair.

key_moments.2.text: The cited finding establishes exceptional length, but does not establish how listeners at the time expected a symphony to run. Say the work was unusually long for a symphony of its time or cite evidence of contemporary expectations.
deep_facts.2.text: The track list does not establish the relative loudness of the Cavatina and the Fifth’s opening movement. Remove the unsupported comparison.

connections.3.connection: The supplied passages identify the work as Goethe’s Egmont and identify Beethoven’s incidental music, but neither identifies Egmont as a play. Cite a source that identifies the genre or say Beethoven composed incidental music for Goethe’s Egmont.

connections.4.connection: The evidence documents a performance during the Congress of Vienna without identifying Beethoven’s role in the performance. Use the documented connection that he composed the cantata for the monarchs and statesmen gathered for the congress, or source the specific performing role.
issues: key_moments.1.text: The supporting passages on suicide refer to renewed commitment to his art and fulfilling his artistic destiny. Use a direct translation to substantiate the claim about music he still wanted to write, or paraphrase this as his wish to continue his work keeping him from taking his own life.

deep_facts.0.text: The obscure detail about how often Beethoven answered aloud and left only the visitor’s words depends on a single Beethoven-Haus catalog account. Seek an independent scholarly account or edition of the conversation books to corroborate this detail.

deep_facts.1.text: The historical invitation underlying the one-versus-thirty-three story is treated as ordinary and supported by one modern catalog account. Corroborate the invitation with an independent scholarly account or surviving publisher material, checking whether the two accounts draw on the same origin. The undisputed count is supported by the work title.

deep_facts.2.text: The unusual Voyager claim relies entirely on three excerpts of one Wikipedia page. Check the two selections against the mission or record documentation and corroborate the claim with an independent original account, checking for copies of the official listing.

connections.1.connection: The finding supports Beethoven setting words from Schiller’s poem, while “which Beethoven set” can imply a setting of the poem as a whole. Say Beethoven used words from it in the Ninth’s finale.

key_moments.1.text: The cited passages document his seclusion and the letter’s despair, but do not show him describing social isolation in the letter itself. Use the Testament text or say he wrote about his worsening hearing and despair.

key_moments.2.text: The cited finding establishes exceptional length, but does not establish how listeners at the time expected a symphony to run. Say the work was unusually long for a symphony of its time or cite evidence of contemporary expectations.
deep_facts.2.text: The track list does not establish the relative loudness of the Cavatina and the Fifth’s opening movement. Remove the unsupported comparison.

connections.3.connection: The supplied passages identify the work as Goethe’s Egmont and identify Beethoven’s incidental music, but neither identifies Egmont as a play. Cite a source that identifies the genre or say Beethoven composed incidental music for Goethe’s Egmont.
